name: The Sins of Grisham Priory
description:
In wretched dimensional backwaters, vicious creatures stalk the blasted landscape and spread sickness, blight and madness through the wider world.

Born of torment and trauma, these Entities are a sickness and a stain on the land.

You, scarred with your own darkness, hunt these monsters.

Hollows is a tactical combat roleplaying game about slaying other people’s personal demons with malevolent Weapons and revelling in the cursed joy of the Hunt.

This Quickstart is intended to give you a taste of the full game by pitching you headlong into a Hollow – a decrepit maze of greed and hunger known as Grisham Priory. Here, you will explore a desolate garden temple complex, meet the broken and dangerous people trapped inside, and destroy the monstrous Entities that rule this rotten place.

incursion.historyText:
Bishop Damien Loxley oversaw the diocese of Grisham, and was renowned for his keen tithe-taking and enforced piety. While acts of service and tending the sacred orchards were all well and good, he knew how the world worked – money, and lots of it. His desire to uplift his charges from poverty through the blessings of the land became an all-consuming obsession with wringing each and every spare penny from those who lived in, or even passed through, his territory. 

Grisham flourished, and Bishop Loxley flourished alongside it. His robes were more splendid than any other clergyman atcourt, his festivals and feasts more lavish, his gardens overflowing with rose and orchid. He did well, and those under his care starved. For decades he was able to shield himself from the harm he was causing, but it couldn’t last forever. One fateful afternoon, when the malnourished peasantry of his parish broke into his priory to find supplies, he lashed out in fury. A dozen men died, and a dozen families were turned out of their hovels for daring to stand against him. 

Something blossomed in Loxley that day. A whisper from the dark between worlds took root in his soul – a revelation. Not onlydid he deserve the riches he had taken, but it was right that he had them. The land had offered up this bounty in exchange for his faith and hard work. Those who would seek to take them are worse than thieves – heretics.

scenes.name: 1. The Graveyard
scenes.notes:
Root: The Bishop sacrifificed a lot of people to get to his lofty position. He never thinks of them at all. 

A dilapidated burial ground. Maybe two hundred graves lie here, with ornamentation ranging from simple wooden effiffigies of pig skulls to great trees carved from marble. Every single one of the graves is anonymous. Here and there, the Hound has dug up a coffiffin or two and eaten the remains, but it looks like very few people have been buried here in recent memory. Before you stands a wide-eyed, haggard-looking occultist clutching a staffff in both their hands. The magic circle they scratched into the dirt is already blowing away. “It worked!” they exclaim. “First things fifirst: take this key.” They thrust a black iron key into your hand with shaking, mud-stained fifingers. “It works on any door,” they continue. “If anything goes wrong, you’ll be safe there.” They pause for a second, exhale, and collect themselves. A relieved smile warms their face. “Where are my manners? My apologies, you can call me –” The doors behind slam open and a hound the size of a carriage lands on them and tears them apart in seconds. It snarls and drags what remains of their broken body back through the doorway. Welcome to the Hollow.

Exit to: Zone 2

scenes.name: 2. The Cloisters
scenes.notes:
Root: The Bishop syphoned resources from his diocese to furnish his estate with lavish trappings while the common folk under his care struggled to survive. 

The people trapped here have erected a makeshift farm in the outdoor space between buildings, but it’s hard going. Tattylooking potato and turnip plants poke through the thin and gritty soil in clumps. Furniture taken from inside the temple has been converted into shelters and barricades – smouldering devotional candelabras teeter precariously atop piles of wardrobes, pews and moth-eaten chaise longues. The entire thing’s a death-trap but they’ve held out until now.

At the centre of the cloister is a shrine covered in images of the dead, painstakingly drawn in charcoal by a careful, shaking hand. This shrine holds the Accusing Ashes; the congregation are unwilling to let them go, as they’re the last remnants of their deceased loved ones. Bargaining, threatening or bribing them could work – attacking them defifinitely will, if you’ve the stomach for it.

Exit to: Zone 3, Zone 4, Zone 5.

scenes.name: 3. The Wormery
scenes.notes:
Root: The Bishop strived to maintain a public image of proper piety, building sacred wormeries, compost heaps and pig farms throughout the district. Anyone who displeased him would wind up as mulch in a matter of months. 

A subterranean warren, dimly lit by candles and braziers. It houses a multitude of floor-to-ceiling interlinked glass boxes filled with decomposing vegetable matter, millions of worms and the occasional skeleton. A whirling mass of worshipers adorned with paper streamers sing the praises of the Bishop and his generosity; on occasion, they form themselves into the shape of a great wyrm with a lit torch at the head, and dance through the maze of glass and dirt. 

Among the material thatmakes up their costumes, a bundle of paper stands out as important – these are the Dolorous Receipts, guarded by these zealots to keep them safe from the Tailor.

Exit to: Zone 2, Zone 5

scenes.name: 4. The Vestry
scenes.notes:
Root: The Tailor had a complicated upbringing and some controversial appetites that would see her cast out of polite society; the Bishop kept receipts of her indiscretions, and used them to blackmail her into his service. 

Silks, bolts of linen and sheets of fifine lace hang from the ceiling in this chamber, but they do little to absorb the noise of the chattering, grinding textile machinery that rattles away of its own accord. Great piles of dye reach as high as the rafters – saffffron yellow, rich purple and boreal green – and man-sized spindles of crimson thread blur with the speed of their ceaseless rotation.

At the centre of this web crouches The Tailor, who endlessly weaves a grand tapestry at the behest of the Bishop. Their vital work interrupted, they lash out at the Hunters as they approach.

Exit to: Zone 2.

scenes.name: 5. The Crypt
scenes.notes:
Root: The Bishop guarded his money, and his secrecy, with the utmost care. 

A crumbling, damp limestone vault carved out of the rock beneath the Temple, with tree-roots questing down from the surface above. The central chamber yawns impossibly tall above the Hunters’ heads; around the entrance, a ward of withered rowan roots has been placed to offffer protection. As the Hunters approach they can hear devotional chanting issuing forth from cracked throats. 

Lining the walls of the structure and enshrined in mausolea are dozens of sarcophagi decorated with statues of the Bishop in repose, as though he has died multiple times. As the Hunters progress through the vault, the caskets become larger, and the statues more monstrous and draconic. Opening any of the graves reveals a skeleton roughly analogous to the statue on top and a smattering of mouldered grave goods. 

At the far end, the monstrous porcine form of The Vicar squats in front of an enormous rusted bank vault door surrounded by ranks of the singing faithful. It’s distracted for now, but it’s in your way.

Exit to: Zone 2, Zone 3, Zone 6

scenes.name: 6. The Root Hole
scenes.notes:
Root: As the Bishop grew in power and influence, he retreated from the public eye and the responsibilities associated with his station. When he finally Hollowed, he had not been seen by anyone other than his closest attendants for months. 

A winding cave system that stretches down far beneath the Priory and deep into the earth. Though parts of it are open enough to stand up straight without banging your head, the majority of the system is made up of cramped tunnels, claustrophobic burrows and partially-flooded passageways. Thankfully, the route down isn’t hard to determine: torn fabric, scuff marks and cracked outcroppings mark frequent passage. 

While the walls start as dirt and mangled masonry, they quickly transition to tightly-packed gold and gems. Cut rubies and jagged emeralds jut out of tunnel walls, a loose scree of bent coins lies precariously underfoot, and tarnished jewellery chain seems to grasp and snare the Hunters as they descend. Near the end of the crawl, a luminescent root shines from the depths of a foot-tall passageway – a Relic.

Exit to: Zone 5, Zone 7

scenes.name: 7. The Golden Pit
scenes.notes:
Root: The Bishop was happy to throw away his faith, his duty and his life in search of greater wealth. 

A network of tunnels dug by claws and loaded with stolen wealth. The floor is lousy with discarded crowns, bent sceptres, dented chalices and torn-up portraits. Huge piles of coins stretch to every wall. Scant illumination is provided by flickering torches mounted in alcoves along the sides of the chamber. Murals, lovingly painted by long-dead hands, depict the Bishop receiving tithes from his diocese – crowds of nobles and peasants alike arrive to shovel money directly into his great distended mouth. 

In the shifting darkness at the centre The Bishop hangs motionless in the shadows, withered arms by his side, gut swollen with gold. As the Hunters approach, they notice an enormous eye open on each side of him, and the truth is revealed: his desiccated remains are protruding from the forehead of the great dragon that he has become in his greed.

identity.factionText:
A people's government bound by bureaucracy and tilting toward civil war.
About a century ago, following pressure from industrialists and exporters, the Crown graciously granted the common folk the right to rule themselves under democratic process and (with great reluctance) nationalised vast swathes of the manufacturing sector. For the first time in written history, over half the Isles were collectively owned by the people who lived and worked there, and no longer under the draconian thrall of a distant monarch. Elected officials worked to better the lives of their constituents, profits were reinvested in the community, and far fewer labourers died due to unsafe machinery or starved to death in the gutter.
Then: the empire collapsed, the work dried up, exports were sunk or blockaded, armies lost war after war on foreign soil, and the House began to cannibalise itself to stay functional. Frantic contracts, desperate promises and vicious threats carved the corpse of the Isles into bloody fragments that changed hands on a monthly basis. A new echelon of Islander arose in the professional politician, proudly severed from the Crown and fiercely working-class, but just as concerned with clinging desperately to power and internecine conflict as the nobles whose rule they refused.
Now, the House is divided into a dozen seats of influence centred around the little industrial infrastructure that remains in the Isles. Responsible for the lives of several million citizens, they function no differently to any other protection racket, although they take pride in citing laws and edicts to back up their violence. In the halls of power, Ministers whisper: the Crown is weak, and their weakness lost them the empire. They damned this country to rust and ruin and they ought to pay. In the streets, tensions rise as gangs of House militia clash with those loyal to the Crown.
The Isles are on the brink of civil war, and the House is hungry for blood.

Hollows:
There are no end of explanations for the rapid decline of the Isles into fractious chaos, and many of them place the blame squarely at the feet of the House's rivals: the insular Viridians, the money-sink that is the Crown, or the meddling weirdos in the Conclave all form convenient scapegoats. The majority of the House have bought into their own propaganda or can't afford to question it too deeply but a devoted core of like-minded obsessives have uncovered the truth behind the infectious corruption, and fight a quiet war to burn it out of the country. Teams of House-sponsored Hunters infiltrate communities on the brink of collapse, with instructions to locate and seal any Hollows they find. These violent and unregulated bands of mercenaries often do more harm than good.

Weapons:
After centuries of the Crown controlling the spread of weapons through the Isles for fear of revolution, the House leapt at the chance to arm every citizen in the nation as an expression of their personal freedom. While the new, mass-produced models of gun, blade and club were less elegant and refined than their handmade ancestors, they were a lot cheaper, and they were perfectly capable of killing any royalist who poked their nose in where it didn't belong. Hunters hailing from the House often use these same bargain-basement Weapons, each well-loved and modified by the bearer the Shotgun, the Pistol, the Knife and the Bludgeon all play a part.
identity.originText:
Armed enforcers, guards and petty tyrants.
Each member of Parliament is permitted by law to maintain a small
militia company who protect their interests and enforce House
regulations. As tensions in the Isles have mounted, the exact legal
definition of a "small company" has been stretched to breaking
point; while most bureaucrats might have an agent or two, senior
ministers have been known to employ hundreds of guards to ensure
their will is carried out. You were in the employ of the House and
you enforced its edicts with blood.
Roll with advantage during exploration when you: intimidate the little
people, stand watch for hours on end, escalate a situation, and so on.

system.coreAbility:
Flourish. Show the beast that you mean business. Once
during your turn you may place 2 Threat on your area to
Feint as an immediate action. Feint is a special action only
available to Sword-wielders.
system.outlook:
The Sword is the King of Weapons. Ancient empires
rose and fell at its point. For millennia, the Sword has
been a symbol of power and authority beyond measure:

a tool for the masters of men to wield with skill and
grace. To cut away the weakest parts of society and to do
what must be done to ensure civilisation's survival and
prosperity.
Fate coalesces around the Sword's point. The Sword
makes myths. It rests in stones waiting for someone
deserving of the honour to rule the kingdom. It severs the
heads of tyrants and rests upon the right hands of great
men. It can elevate a common citizen to knighthood with
but a touch.
Next to the Sword, the frantic fear of the Knife and the
Spear fall away to nothing. The brutish Bludgeon falters
and stumbles. The Book is cut to shreds, the Staff sliced
in twain, the Armour rent asunder and the sound and fury
of the firearm silenced. It gladly bears the burden laid
upon its shoulders - someone's got to do it. Someone has
to lead the charge.
system.lies:
The Sword believes in heroes in the ancient sense of
the word. It wants to convince its wielders that they
stand proudly ahead of their peers: that there are those
who are born to lead, thanks to some indefinable spark of
greatness deep within their being, and it is their duty to
shepherd the people beneath them.
But the glorious ages of the past have died. The world
has grown sour and corrupt, and the concepts of which
the Sword sings - honour, duty, nobility and sacrifice -
are twisted and withered things. It spits hate on the
feckless masses and preaches exceptionalism. It tells you:
you alone are meant for greatness. These pitiful creatures
are nothing without you to lead them. You are worthy of
the respect you see glinting in their bovine eyes.
system.fears:
The Sword's time in the sun is over, and it clings to
what little relevance it retains. As the rifle and the
field gun scar the globe into new and terrible empires, the
Sword sees their eyes on the throne. It feels itself slipping
into rite and ritual as it becomes a relic of bygone days.
The Sword only matters if the people know it matters. Its
authority is not innate, but granted with conditions. Spears
outreach it. Knives carve and craft and make. It glances off
Armour's skin and every single gun outranges it.
So it speaks of honourable combat. It admonishes those
who fight dirty and births schools of duellists, manuals
of techniques, and reams of rules designed to fashion
the grim business of ending lives into something that
demands admiration and grace. It is desperate to dictate
the battlefield and hold onto its unfair advantage, because
without it, it is nothing but a length of sharpened steel.

system.outlook:
The Pistol is chief amongst the new gods of bloodshed;
gunpowder and lead put a lightning strike in the
palm of the everyman, and almost every hero of every
story now clutches a handgun at some point in the tale.
Where clergymen would bless swords, they now pray
over pistols and ask the gods to guide the shooter's hand.
Advertisements on street corners and the back pages of
periodicals boast of skull-cracking strength, quick-draw
designs and affordable ammunition.
The Sword has been replaced as a mark of personal
prowess - no longer do you have to train for years to use
a weapon, or risk your skin by coming close to those you
want to hurt. Anyone with a few quid and a vendetta can
set the odds in their favour with a Pistol in their pocket.
system.lies:
The Pistol tells you: you're the best there is. No-one
has what you've got; you're unique, and special, and
fascinating. The world is chaotic and unfocused but you,
Pistol gripped against your skin, rise above the noise and
move unfettered.
A lack of success or prosperity should be no indication that
maybe you've overestimated yourself; instead, it's everyone
else's fault that you've not made it yet. Your ideas are too
new, too revolutionary, to be accepted. Anyone who passes
you over or looks down on you knows the truth: they're
jealous of your ability and scared of what you might do.
This absolute refusal to change based on new
information brings with it a bullet-proof confidence, and
the Pistol wants to propel its bearers forward into the
future on the back of it. Reality is what you make it, and
you're the guy holding the gun.
system.fears:
Ignore the flash and the posturing. The Pistol believes
that it isn't supposed to be here, but as long as no-one
else finds out, it's fine. It's fine.
It's not an instrument of war; no great glories, no stern
sacrifices, no tactical masterstrokes owe it thanks. It's not a
tool for hunting, either; thick hides turn aside little bullets,
rifles outrange it, and it's a coward's crutch next to the cut
and thrust of finishing the beast with blade and bludgeon.
It's not a part of anything greater, or ancient, or more noble.
No abstraction or artifice masks it with the sacrosanct.
All it does is kill people. Is that enough? Is the Pistol
enough?
It spins stories of its own prowess and whispers feverish
in the ears of those who carry it: you're the best, you're
the greatest, you're streets ahead of these fools. It keeps
everyone and everything at arm's length. It never shows
an ounce of weakness or confusion if it can help it. The
alternative is unthinkable; a crash and burn, a dethroning,
and a cold eternity of exile. Better to keep up the act
forever than run the risk of discovery.

identity.factionText:
Disparate occult scholars trying to tackle rhyme with reason
Hundreds of doctors, scientists, academics, sorcerers and divinators have sworn their allegiance to the Conclave because they share the same core philosophy: the world is not ready to accept the truth. Nestled between bloodlines, hiding behind legislation and edict, alluded to in apocrypha and woven throughout the fabric of the Isles, the Conclave has carefully guided the development of the country for the last thousand years.
They operate on principles of containment and analysis. Strange data, subjects and materials still-living rustwood harvested from Hollows, reports of interdimensional breaches, malformed refugees from curdled otherworlds are bundled away from prying eyes and jabbed, tested, probed and disassembled in order to learn as much as possible about them.
Given that Hollows are both born of trauma and spread that same trauma, it is possible for them to spread memetically through a population, so the Conclave are careful to the point of paranoia, some would say to maintain a distance between those exposed to the information and those blissfully unaware. They take great pains to secret themselves away from society at large (and each other) in sanctums, towers, dungeons, catacombs, forts, barrows and pits anywhere remote and defensible. The more important a member of the Conclave is, the less other adherents will see them, and the upper echelons are so mysterious and isolationist that many of them may well be invented from whole cloth as a distraction.
Since their creation by an ancient queen over a millennium ago, the Conclave has zealously maintained its original aim: to understand the supernatural forces that predate humanity, and eventually to counteract those forces once and for all by revealing the truth to the world. Of late, there have been mutterings of a breakthrough that they have discovered a path through to the domains of the Malignancies themselves, and a way for Hunters to survive direct contact with these vast and ravenous monsters.
Not everyone is convinced of the group's noble mission. Detractors say that the Conclave is a splintered, amoral, directionless bunch of hermits scrabbling for power in the ruins of the empire no better than everyone else. In fact, only one in six or so members possesses a solid grasp of the arcane arts, thanks to a dedicated effort on the inner circle's part to portion out sensitive information in useless fragments. The rest of the rank-and-file members are desperate posers, occult hobbyists, deluded madmen, educated hucksters, and gullible rubes.

Hollows:
The Conclave has a unique interest in the parasitic snickets that plague the populace they look to harvest their secrets, and turn them to their own ends. There are tricks which allow those without a Seed to step within a Hollow's borders, and wards of protection both ancient and modern give them a chance of surviving the experience. Given that only a scant handful of their number can enter Hollows without great risk or expense, the Conclave often relies on teams of sponsored Hunters to collect information and relics from within.
Working for the Conclave is no easy matter; they are demanding masters, and their obsession with cataloguing and exploiting Malignancies leads them to make strange requests. Where other sponsors may be happy to see Hollows merely burnt out and destroyed, Conclave Hunters are frequently tasked with capturing or interrogating Entities: a much more challenging prospect, and one that calls into question the nature of these beings in ways that may give their abductors pause.

Weapons:
With their inherent connection to the occult, the Book and Staff are the primary tools of the Conclave; they give wielders the power to control, subvert and overwhelm the strange reality of a Hollow. The esoteric nature of the group's recruitment processes (and the individual idiosyncrasies of its members) result in a variety of unusual Weapons weighty recurved Swords, bone-handled ritual Knives, and long-barrelled Pistols covered in spiralling script or laden with experimental improvements.
identity.originText:
Medical curiosities and aberrations.
Destitute and desperate, you submitted yourself to experimentation
and went under the keen knives of the Conclave. After the
experiments concluded, you were left with a network of scars,
resonant metals implanted under your skin, and an uncanny
sense of the Malignancies that gnaw ravenous at the Isles. You've
been haunted by visions of unreal worlds and monsters beyond
reckoning but you believe you can find peace by delving headlong
into the nightmare and bleeding it dry.
Roll with advantage during exploration when you: use your
unnatural senses, withstand punishment or torture, escape a dire
situation, and so on.

system.coreAbility:
Bleeding. Let the life drain from its veins. When you inflict
a Wound with the Knife, the Entity begins Bleeding.
Place the Bleeding token next to the Entity as a reminder.
Bleeding is treated as a separate damage source, so can't
be boosted by abilities that affect a Hunter's damage, and
does not trigger Threat placement.
At the start of the Entity's turn, a Bleeding Entity
suffers 2 Resolve damage or, if it is Broken, 1 Wound
damage. Then, toss the Bleeding token like a coin. If it
shows Bleeding, the Entity retains the Bleeding status.
If it shows Whole, the Bleeding status is removed.
When the Entity restores Resolve, it also removes
Bleeding.
An Entity is either Bleeding or not. Bleeding cannot
be applied twice at the same time, and Bleeding damage
does not stack and is only inflicted once per round.
Bleeding persists if the Knife-wielding Hunter dies,
along with any passive abilities which apply while the
Entity is Bleeding, until it is removed.
system.outlook:
The Knife is the perpetual underdog. Every
warrior in every army throughout history has
carried a Knife, but they carried a proper Weapon
too. Something you can wave around and threaten
people with, something with a bit of heft behind it,
something you can hang on the wall when you come
back from the chaos. Something that means business.
The Knife wants to show those bastards that it
means business.
It's sharp. One cut will kill you. No hustle and
bluster; nothing but blood.
It's everywhere. It's in every house in the kingdom,
every pocket in the street. It's out of the shadows and
at their throats. No-one sees it coming.
And it's personal. You kill something with a Knife,
you have to want it dead. You open yourself up to
attack. You grip white-knuckled to the fucker and
stab until your arms ache. By the end, you're soaked
in scarlet. You earn your kill.

The Knife knows that the world is out to get you.

way you look, or who your parents were, or what side
of the river you grew up on. The odds were stacked
against you before you even drew a card. At every
turn, someone's arrived to steal what you've fought so
hard for without giving you a second thought.
You're not the aggressor, says the Knife: you're
taking revenge. Every drop of blood is justified. They
and theirs have kept you down for too long; you need
to fight back and take what you're owed. Your only
mistake was not doing it sooner.
If you win, you're a hero. If you lose, you were never
supposed to succeed. There's a comfort in occupying
the bottom rung, especially when it opens your
enemies up to retribution.

Some of the bearers that the Knife chooses are, in
fact, the sort of embittered underdogs it believes
them to be - but many aren't. They wear their
imagined persecution as a badge of honour and think
that, if so many people are dead-set against them,
they must be doing something revolutionary to shake
up the status quo.
The Knife is scared of not being underestimated.

wake, singing your praises, carrying your kit and paying you
tithes. You are their champion, leading the fight against those
they despise, protecting that which they value. You want
them to believe they're dependent on you.

The Rifle conquered the world. When the dominion
of the Isles was at its height, it was at the heart of
every conquering force: trade and diplomacy may be
what cements an empire in place, but violence digs the
foundations. The Rifle was the perfect tool for the job:
accurate, reliable, and deadly. The long barrel and heavy
charge of gunpowder let soldiers engage with the enemy
at a respectable distance - no swirling melee, no barbaric
brawling, but a measured march towards victory. With a
Rifle, you can kill a man and never see the fear in his eyes,
or smell the stench of death, or hear the last breath stutter
staccato out of his foaming mouth.
But one Rifle doesn't win a war; ten thousand Rifles
do. To deliver ten thousand Rifles - and the ammunition
needed to fire them, and the tools to maintain them, and
the spare parts to swap out during a campaign, and the
soldiers to carry them - you need infrastructure. You need
steel refineries and weapons manufacturers and cargo ships
and iron ore mines and anti-union laws and strikebreakers
and vassal nations and bloodlines and flags and the
continual threat, whether implied or explicit, of absolute
violence against those who disagree with you. You need
civilisation.
The Rifle is the foremost, sharpest point of the grand
machine that was the empire.
system.lies:
Stand up straight and walk tall - you've earned it. A life
of hard work and good decisions, backed up by the
hard work and good decisions of your forefathers, sets
you apart from the rest. You've earned your money, your
comfort, your security.
You are untouchable, unimpeachable, unflappable. You
can do whatever you want because you are in charge and
whatever you want is the right thing to do. Those who think
differently to you are weak, immoral, bestial, petty, deluded.
Things instead of people.
You're the conquering army. You're the state. You're the
rules. You're the boys' club, the back-room deal, the secret
handshake, the right choice made at the right time with the
right people. You cannot be stopped.

What use is a Rifle without bullets? What happens when
the sights misalign, when the mechanism jams, when
the bolt sticks in the chamber or the powder's too wet to fire?
It's just dead weight to carry around - an obligation you've
brought upon yourself and that you're too proud to forsake.
The Rifle is scared of being unsupported and alone -
away from supply lines, from convenience and comfort,
from those it deems peer or peon. It knows that, if left
alone and told to manifest its destiny, it's dead in the water.
It needs everything underneath it ticking like clockwork to
even survive.

identity.factionText:
A flourishing religious movement that preaches endless bounty.
The Isles have a long and uneasy relationship with the supernatural. Before the rise of the empire, the average Islander believed that a pantheon of malevolent gods and spirits were ever-ready to punish them for obscure transgressions against inscrutable laws. Ramshackle amalgamations of folk beliefs coalesced into a broad tradition of fear, obfuscation and appeasement; churches were not places to honour the gods, but carefully-maintained divine blind spots where important events (births, marriages, festivals, funerals) could be safely conducted out of their sight.
The empire smashed it all asunder. The relentless march of industrialisation upturned the fragmentary faith. War, hungry for sacrifice, sent whole villages to the front and unattended churches fell to ruin.
The upstart gardeners of the Viridian Temple seized the moment: they preached that the gods were not vicious creatures, but instead dead and rotting beneath the ground, providing sustenance for the world to come. Heaven was no distant realm of light or chthonic purgatory but could rise from the earth itself with careful guidance.
An uprooted populace, battered and bruised from millennia of terror, were ready for a new message. Viridian Temple Gardens sprang up all across the Isles in the lost farms and villages, amidst the smoke and fire of cities, on rooftop and ship deck, in the ruins of fallen churches and behind each fresh military expansion overseas. Viridian morality plays and holy texts flooded the market with the good word. Temple schools taught children to read and write and fed them, and clothed them, and burned the prophecies of plenty into their malleable minds.
Now, the majority of the food supply for the Isles is controlled by the Viridians. The other factions in power don't always see eye to eye with the gardeners, but they toe the line. More than one political enemy has been buried under an orchard, chopped up and fed to sacred pigs, or bonfire-burnt like a parasite weed.

Hollows:
As the gods rot beneath the soil, their metaphysical putrefaction escapes and catches in this earthly kingdom to form Hollows tenacious and invasive weeds that must be plucked before they take root and spread in the minds and bodies of the congregation. While the majority of the faithful don't give much credence to the existence of parasite dimensions, someone in the upper ranks certainly does, as the church has instituted an aggressive outreach program with an eye to monitoring those at risk of blossoming into something terrible. Whether the sufferer is brought back into the fold or quietly removed, prevention is seen to be better than cure and employing teams of Hunters to demolish Hollows is the sign of a church that failed to do its duty.

Weapons:
Traditional tools of farming and animal husbandry turned to violent ends, or modified to be more dangerous, are popular amongst adherents to the Viridian faith. The Knife, the Staff, the Bludgeon and the Spear are all common Weapons amongst their number, and when it comes to ending the life of an injured or belligerent beast, the Shotgun is often the kindest method. Bearers will often augment or modify their Weapons with materials taken from the natural world skulls, thorns, leathers, wool and flowers are common decorations.
The Book is also present in the form of sacred texts that speak of dominion over the natural world and contain useful guidance on crop rotation, care of livestock, treating most common diseases and, of course, performing actual magic spells.
identity.originText:
Itinerant holy folk in charge of sacred beasts.
The domesticated pig is held in the highest regard by the Viridians a
perfect omnivorous beast, fat from the bounty of the land, ripe and
ready for the slaughter. Orthodox adherents proclaim that pigs should
not be kept behind fences or cages but instead allowed to roam the
country as they please, eating unobstructed, and permitted access
to whatever field, storehouse or pantry they barge their way into.
You were a Swineherd, a well-respected and enviable position within
the church, and you spent years wandering the land and contemplating
the divine corpulence and ineffable wisdom of your charges.
Roll with advantage during exploration when you: interact with
animals, get up to your elbows in mud and shit, persuade someone to
let you into their private land, etc.

system.coreAbility:
Loaded. All or nothing. The Shotgun doesn?t have Capacity
like other ranged Weapons. Instead, it is either Empty
or Loaded. At the start of each fight, the Shotgun is
Loaded: place the Shotgun token on your character
sheet with the Loaded side up. While it?s Loaded, you
can make an attack by flipping it to Empty; while it?s
Empty, you can make a Reload manoeuvre to flip it to
Loaded. You can only make attacks with the Shotgun
while it is Loaded. You may only use the sections of your
abilities matching the current state of your Weapon.
In general, effects that restore Capacity also allow you
to flip the Shotgun from Empty to Loaded.
system.outlook:
The Shotgun (or blunderbuss, or dragon, or
scattergun, or coach gun) uses a sizeable charge
to fire multiple projectiles at a target. On the upside,
the spread of shot means that accuracy is no longer a
concern - on the downside, the laborious process of
loading the ammunition leaves the bearer vulnerable to
attack once they've pulled the trigger.
It is not a new or complicated concept. Whilst
the Rifle and Pistol have made recent advances with
regards to accuracy, capacity and rate of fire, the
Shotgun has been perfectly happy to blast great clouds
of debris downrange for centuries with very little
change in its construction. It is easy to make, easy to
use, and you can fire pretty much anything out of it
and still make an impact.
It is immediate and indiscriminate violence in physical
form. It promises absolute destruction at the pull of
a trigger: an attack without patience or restraint that
sends even the fiercest foe reeling.
system.lies:
What if, the Shotgun asks, you no longer held
back? The world is a web of carefully-maintained
social constructs designed to hold our baser impulses in
check and, not coincidentally, keep power in the hands
of those who already possess it. The game is rigged
from the start, but you don't have to play it. There's an
advantage in being the wild card, and to ignore all the
restrictions and boundaries placed upon you. To do the
unthinkable. To kill and maim and ruin.
Certainly intimidation and fear have their place, but
that's not what the blood-hungry Shotgun is interested
in. It wants action. It wants to blow the world clean
in half and relish in the aftermath. It wants to break
things to prove that they can be broken. Violence is the
only form of communication that matters, and you've
got the ultimate solution to any given problem: death.
system.fears:
Death is not the ultimate solution to any problem.
The Shotgun knows this.
Those carefully-maintained social constructs can't
be torn asunder so easily. The Shotgun doesn't like to
think about what happens after the shot is fired and
the smoke clears; that it is empty, and powerless, and
open to retribution.
It hates being unloaded, and it hates not being fired.
What it desires is impossible and intoxicating: no
waiting and no need for recovery, but only an endless
instant of fury. It exists solely for that brief moment of
fire and noise and the fleeting taste of absolute power.
The lies it tells are wild and unsustainable, but to the
right person, they'll hold together long enough.

system.outlook:
The Book is the latest form of an ancient concept -
knowledge, materialised, that can be shared or jealously
hoarded. What is now paper and ink was once chiselled
tablets of stone or rich pigment daubed across the walls of
firelit caves. It sees the world not as a chaotic mess, but instead
a series of rules which can be manipulated to its advantage.
The Book's violence is more subtle than that of its
companions in the Weapons' bloodstained pantheon. Every
Weapon is a tool through which humans impose their will
upon the world, and where the others may do so directly
with fire and iron, the Book holds itself above such base
matters. Violence is not only the crack of bone and tang
of blood; pure violence, unsullied by the sweat and pain of
the melee, is the subjugation of that which you deem to be
beneath you. The Book knows that everything is beneath it.
system.lies:
The Old Faith spoke of the power of words. Their
godlings possessed true names that could be used to
control them by simply being spoken aloud, and the Book
sees the wisdom in this concept. Let others grunt and strain
to make an impact; to understand something is to control it.
Absolute truth is not only possible but extant, and it lies
within the pages of the Book. Where others stumble around in
darkness, you have the intellect and the determination to pierce
the veil of ignorance and see the world for what it really is.
Not only that; when you impose structure on the world
around you, you give it a form pleasing to your eye. You
create species and periodic tables, constellations and
countries, ethnicities and social classes, heretics and saints.
Everything you see is yours to control and order with you,
bright and brilliant as the sun, at the centre.
system.fears:
The thought that the Book might be one day disproved fills it
with an existential dread. It cannot allow any part of itself to
become false; to do so would be to invalidate its entire existence.
Once conjecture coalesces into truth, that truth becomes
brittle and breakable. The stern wisdom that the Book
provides offers no quarter and permits no incursion upon its
sanctity. Those who build their foundations upon the Book's
truth are moral and sensible and good; those who offer an
alternative viewpoint are, logically (and the Book loves logic)
immoral, foolish, and evil. Genuine truths do not bend and
adapt in the presence of conflicting evidence, but instead
must be defended against deluded and malicious agents hellbent on their destruction.
It isn't stupid. It knows that, from the moment its final
page is written, any insight it offers becomes less relevant.
Contexts shift and erode. Touchstones crumble, idioms
invert themselves, and audiences die out. The Book is true
only as long as people believe it is, and that truth - the only
truth the Book can really guarantee - is at the root of its
implacable refusal to compromise.

system.outlook:
The Spear is, in all likelihood, the oldest man-made weapon
in existence. It has evolved from a length of wood that's
sharper on one end than it is on the other to a panoply of

polearms that defined the shape of warfare for thousands of
years. Whilst it lacks the idealism attached to the Sword or
the utility bound up in the Knife, the Spear was the weapon of
choice for the common soldier until upstart firearms arrived and
pushed it off the top spot.
The ubiquity and archaic nature of the Spear makes it
unfashionable, but the Spear doesn't mind. The Spear was there
at the dawn of time when the first humans decided that they
wanted to bring down beasts ten times their size, or to stab
someone whilst staying out of stabbing range themselves. The
Spear predates machines, structures, clothing, the written word,
language, and numeracy. The Spear has watched the rise and fall
of other pretenders - the aloof longbow, the cackling crossbow,
the spiteful warhammer - and knows that it will be here long after
the cities have crumbled to dust and the last bullet has been fired.
system.lies:
The Spear knows that the home - the hearth, the space you claim
as your own - is sacred. It wants to help you keep it sacred by
ensuring the profane - which is to say anything you decide you don't
like - is excluded by force. To breach the sacred is unthinkable,
and anyone who would even consider it should be destroyed.
"Home", of course, is a malleable concept. Home can be the house
in which you live, but it can be your church. Your town. Your nation.
Your kingdom. Wherever people who look like you exist. Wherever
people who share your ideals make a stand. When it comes to
Hollows, an entire plane of reality - as battered and bruised as it is -
can be a home, and worth defending. The Spear doesn't like to think
of itself as attacking. Anything the Spear does is defence, no matter
how pre-emptive it might seem or if it has to be carried over borders
and jammed in some poor bastard's guts to do it.
You are supposed to be here. You are entitled to occupy this
space, and furthermore, you are entitled to everything within
it. Anyone you let inside is yours to protect, but yours to use as
you will, and can be expelled whenever you please. They owe you
their life, after all.
system.fears:
The Spear is terrified of being abandoned. Although it is
very picky about who it lets inside what it considers to be
home, it knows (but would hesitate to say) that it needs others
to survive. What good is a King who is reliant on his subjects?
What good is a man who cannot protect his family with his own
strength and cunning alone?
It brags of sole mastery over its domain - of permissions granted
and contracts bestowed, of sworn oaths and kind allowances - but
dreads the day that its power is found wanting and those under its
protection are killed, or worse, decide to leave before it is ready to
let them go. The crossed spears, a symbol of barring and refusal,
are just as frequently used against those under the Spear's authority
as they are against those who stand against it.

The Hound is a simple beast: a physical manifestation of the Bishop’s frantic desire to protect what he believes to be his. It takes the form of a grotesquely-muscled dog – half-pitbull, half-wolfhound – and stands taller than a man at the shoulder. You get to place 4 Threat at the end of your turn, so make sure to use it to trigger Snap and Snarl as often as possible or enhance Grab and Shake. She hangs in the centre of a maze of cloth and rattling machinery; every thundering loom, every dashing needle, every whirring wheel is a part of her and moves with an imperfect, stuttering grace.

text.content:
Grisham Priory

Content Warnings

Dogs, animal attacks, dragons, spider analogues, poverty, starvation, cruelty to animals, needles, religion and religious violence.

The Tale

Bishop Damien Loxley oversaw the diocese of Grisham, and was renowned for his keen tithe-taking and enforced piety. While acts of service and tending the sacred orchards were all well and good, he knew how the world worked – money, and lots of it. His desire to uplift his charges from poverty through the blessings of the land became an all-consuming obsession with wringing each and every spare penny from those who lived in, or even passed through, his territory.

Grisham flourished, and Bishop Loxley flourished alongside it. His robes were more splendid than any other clergyman at court, his festivals and feasts more lavish,
his gardens overflowing with rose and orchid. He did well, and those under his care starved. For decades he was able to shield himself from the harm he was causing, but it couldn’t last forever. One fateful afternoon, when the malnourished peasantry of his parish broke into his priory to find supplies, he lashed out in fury. A dozen men died, and a dozen families were turned out of their hovels for daring to stand against him.

Something blossomed in Loxley that day. A whisper from the dark between worlds took root in his soul – a revelation. Not only did he deserve the riches he had taken, but it was right that he had them. The land had offered up this bounty in exchange for his faith and hard work. Those who would seek to take them are worse than thieves – heretics.

Personal Hells, Made To Order

Each Hollow has a Tale – the genesis of the seed planted in the Lord by one of the Grand Malignancies that circle the Isles like carrion crows. As with the Roots that come later on in each individual zone, these are designed to give the GM some background on the events that lead to the hollowing and help them roleplay and invent details on the fly.

Strange Things

Each Hollow is accompanied by a collection of Strange Things that can be useful when describing the Hollow to your players. They often foreshadow future Entities or locations, and are provided to aid the GM in adding colour and flair to their descriptions of the Hollow.

  • A coin bounces and rolls through a crack in the floor.

  • Webs of fine red thread form trip-wires across thoroughfares.

  • Porcelain fungi sprout from the desiccated earth.

  • The wall is worn thin, revealing stained glass portraits beneath the stone.

  • A thrall begs for food that they cannot draw nourishment from.

  • A thin, greasy flurry of rain spatters against a window or roof.

  • A song of praise to the Bishop echoes down a corridor.

  • Your Weapon refuses to draw blood unless it’s “paid”.

  • A bloated pig, dressed with ribbons and prayers,
    farts and snorts its way through the Hollow in search of food.

  • The ceiling collapses after decades of disrepair.

Priory Background

Sometimes while roleplaying, you might want to introduce additional encounters or rewards for your players. Here are some incidental items and hazards that your players might find while exploring, in addition to (or instead of) the relics that are associated with specific areas and inhabitants of the Hollow. Bear in mind that introducing new Hazards or Relics can change the game balance in significant ways; consider introducing them if your players are having a hard (or too easy) time.

Supplementary Relics

Brittle Riches. Forgotten gold that turns to ash when touched. One use. While in Close, as an immediate action in response to a target being declared, you may cancel one Entity attack. This attack has no effect but still incurs any costs.

Beautiful Silks. Once the height of fashion, now best for binding wounds. One use. As a Use action, you may heal 2 Wounds to an ally in your area.

Supplementary Hazards

Fervent worshippers. The misguided often fight the hardest. Hard TN6. Damage 1/1. Health 2/2.

Pacing Yourselves

In the core Hollows game, most Hollows will have a Doom track that goes up to 25. In this quickstart, we’ve provided a shorter track and a more immediate first combat, to get you into the action more quickly.

The Hunters will accrue Doom through exploration, so the longer they take to explore the more risky their eventual battles will become. But on the other hand, they’ll know more about the Lord and its Vassals, and maybe even have access
to valuable tools they can use to change the fight. It’s up to you as a group to decide how many risks to take in discovering the story of this place.

DOOM

3 Awakened Senses . Replace the Tailor’s Vicious Webability with: Awakened Senses. Target any area with less than 4 Threat. Shift up to 4 Threat to that area.

5 Improvised Barricades.Increase the Vicar’s Ranged defence to 10.

7 Trapdoor Tailor. Hunters begin the Tailor fight with 1 Curse each.

8 Ceremonial Armour. Increase the Bishop’s Resolve to 9.

9 Fell Curses. The Vicar’s Bellowing Prayermanoeuvre is now Wise TN10, 3/1.

10 Overconfident. Replace the Bishop’s Flee manoeuvre with: Scurry. Restore X Resolve, where X is 6 minus 1 for each Hunter at Close.

11 Death Trap. The Tailor’s Threat Cap is increased to 14.

12 Swell The Ranks. While the Vicar is not Broken, it makes an immediate Advisory Committeemanoeuvre at the start of each of its turns.

13 Undermine. The Bishop gains the following ability: When First Broken: Undermine. Coins roar in the depths. Make a Money Sink attack targeting two adjacent areas. This attack does not cost Threat.

15 Doom. If the Doom track is full, the Bishop immediately attacks the Hunters. Begin the battle. If all the Hunters are slain during this fight, reduce Doom by 3 and continue.

Entering the Hollow

There are a hundred ways and more to enter a Hollow. Some Hunters rely on arcane tools like black scrying mirrors, rune-etched pendulums, or ritual candles; some weaken the barrier between worlds with sacred earth, rowan roots and devil’s-salt then force their way through; some converse with the lost spirit of the Hollowed, or pose as a loved one, and con their way inside.

This time, you were pulled in. As you prepared to make your entrance, the world stuttered and cracked around you, and reality seared with burning sigils and fell away.

The Hollow takes the form of an overgrown church complex; you appear in front of a great door that seals it off from storm-blasted wastes that stretch away in every direction.

You are in…

1. The Graveyard

Root: The Bishop sacrificed a lot of people to get to his lofty position. He never thinks of them at all.

A dilapidated burial ground. Maybe two hundred graves lie here, with ornamentation ranging from simple wooden effigies of pig skulls to great trees carved from marble. Every single one of the graves is anonymous. Here and there, the Hound has dug up a coffin or two and eaten the remains, but it looks like very few people have been buried here in recent memory.

Before you stands a wide-eyed, haggard-looking occultist clutching a staff in both their hands. The magic circle they scratched into the dirt is already blowing away.

“It worked!” they exclaim.

“First things first: take this key.” They thrust a black iron key into your hand with shaking, mud-stained fingers.

“It works on any door,”they continue. “If anything goes wrong, you’ll be safe there.” They pause for a second, exhale, and collect themselves. A relieved smile warms their face.

“Where are my manners? My apologies, you can call me –”

The doors behind slam open and a hound the size of a carriage lands on them and tears them apart in seconds. It snarls and drags what remains of their broken body back through the doorway.

Welcome to the Hollow.

The First Combat

The Quickstart begins with a battle against the Guardian Hound (page 38), a vassal Entity. Show the players the tactical grid and have them roll for placement and turn order (page 12) against the Hound’s Ranged Defence of 12.

First, the group of Hunters who act before the Entity take their turns (page 16). After every Hunter turn ends, you may (and should!) make an Interrupt action if you are able to spend Threat to do so.

Then, you take the Entity’s turn (page 18). At the end of your turn, place Threat equal to the Entity’s Threat Per Turn (page 19).

After that, the remaining Hunters take their turns. You may make Interrupt actions after these turns as well.

Once all the Hunters have acted, the first round is over and a new round begins. Continue until the Guardian Hound is killed and perform your first Baptism (page 22). In the unlikely event all the Hunters die, they awaken in the Sanctum (page 34).

Introductions

The first round of combat is a great time to get your players to introduce their characters. If you like, ask each one to describe their physical appearance as they square up against the Entity, and tell the group a little about how their Weapons look and behave as they use them. Big showy cinematic descriptions of combat aren’t to everyone’s taste, but they can really enhance the way the game feels to play, and help your players feel ownership over their new Hunters.

Baptism, Healing & Advancement

After the Hound is defeated, the players receive a Baptism: they are imbued with a small portion of the Entity’s power, which allows them to restore their Resolve to full, heal some Wounds, and advance. Each Hunter alive at the end of the battle restores their Resolve to its maximum value, then rolls Hard; on a success, they restore Wounds to maximum, and on a failure they restore Wounds to half their maximum value, rounding up.

Each Hunter involved in the Battle – whether living or dead at the end – may choose one new Weapon ability. Hunters advance in this way after every successful Battle.

Tracking Doom

Now the Hound is dead, you'll want to start tracking Doom. It starts at zero, and is increased when the players fail Exploration rolls or open doors into the Sanctum. As it increases, it makes combat more challenging. You might want to describe it as a sense of foreboding, or in terms of the supernatural strangeness of this place intensifying, using the Strange Things list on page 30 as a guide.

Entity Rewards

In general, Entities in Hollows don’t grant equipment as loot; instead, they grant Balm, Blood and Bone.

Balm restores all Hunters back up to their maximum Resolve and gives them an opportunity to heal Wounds.

Blood is a rush of power that floods into the Hunters and takes up residence in their Weapons, unlocking new abilities within them. Describe this however works for you: mystical energy, light or darkness, smoke, thick ichor, whisperings from the Weapons, or trinkets taken from the corpse and tied to the Hunters’ Weapons.

Bone represents physical tokens that carry a small part of the Entity’s power, ossified into solid form. In this Quickstart, there is no way to spend these resources, but if you’d like to continue the game beyond this scenario – or your players want some loot as a reward – describe the dog’s collar, a hank of its hair, or a chunk of its chain, thrumming with dark power and begging to be carried.

The Sanctum

Buried within the walls of the Priory is the Sanctum – the paradimensional foxhole that Varrick, the occultist who pulled the Hunters into the Hollow, is holed up inside. The Sanctum is a cramped, wood-panelled room with mould on the walls and flagstone flooring. Several pews have been dragged together to form a sort of makeshift bed against one wall.

The Hunters can insert the key that Varrick gave them into any door; doors that lack keyholes will morph one into being in response to the key’s proximity. The door now opens into the Sanctum instead of its original location. The creatures from the Priory cannot enter here.

If the Hunters are eager to discover more about the key after the Guardian Hound fight, encourage them to explore among the mausoleums of the Graveyard, or suggest that the key pulls on their fingers as they approach the door to the next area, the Cloisters.

When the Hunters enter, they restore their Resolve and Wounds to their starting values as they catch their breath and bandage their injuries.

After dying, a Hunter will wake up here with their Resolve and Wounds restored to their starting values.

Whenever a Hunter opens the door to the Sanctum, no matter how many Hunters pass through, add 3 Doom to reflect the time and supernatural disturbance involved.

Varrick is hiding out here, and they are terrified of leaving the Sanctum; although they too come back to life here if they die in the Hollow, they’re feeling increasingly unstable after a dozen deaths. The next one might be their last, and then they’d blossom into a Hollow all their very own.

Take Refuge

In the full Hollows game, players gain access to their own sanctum – a snicket in space and time, known as the Refuge. In time, they’ll be able to welcome in other lost souls, construct new rooms and arcane devices, augment and improve their abilities and stats, and even rescue the tormented souls of Lords to live in peace via Anchoring.

2. The Cloisters

Root: The Bishop syphoned resources from his diocese to furnish his estate with lavish trappings while the common folk under his care struggled to survive.

The people trapped here have erected a makeshift farm in the outdoor space between buildings, but it’s hard going. Tatty-looking potato and turnip plants poke through the thin and gritty soil in clumps. Furniture taken from inside the temple has been converted into shelters and barricades – smouldering devotional candelabras teeter precariously atop piles of wardrobes, pews and moth-eaten chaise longues. The entire thing’s a death-trap but they’ve held out until now.

At the centre of the cloister is a shrine covered in images of the dead, painstakingly drawn in charcoal by a careful, shaking hand. This shrine holds the Accusing Ashes; the congregation are unwilling to let them go, as they’re the last remnants of their deceased loved ones. Bargaining, threatening or bribing them could work – attacking them definitely will, if you’ve the stomach for it.

The Viridian
Congregation

A pathetic rabble, the tatters of the congregation.

Strong TN7. Damage 2/2. Health 4/4. Dealing with them gives the Hunters the Accusing Ashes.

Accusing Ashes

Blessed ashes of
those who starved due to the Bishop’s insatiable greed.

One Use. As a Use action: in Close, reduce one of the Entity’s Defences by 2. Effective against any Entity within Grisham Priory.

Relics

The presence of a Relic is immediately obvious to any Hunter; they look different from everything else around them, weighed down as they are with power. If a Hunter collects a Relic, tell them what it does in mechanical terms. There’s no need to be coy and mysterious about it.

3. The Wormery

Root: The Bishop strived to maintain a public image of proper piety, building sacred wormeries, compost heaps and pig farms throughout the district. Anyone who displeased him would wind up as mulch in a matter of months.

A subterranean warren, dimly lit by candles and braziers. It houses a multitude of floor-to-ceiling interlinked glass boxes filled with decomposing vegetable matter, millions of worms and the occasional skeleton. A whirling mass of worshipers adorned with paper streamers sing the praises of the Bishop and his generosity; on occasion, they form themselves into the shape of a great wyrm with a lit torch at the head, and dance through the maze of glass and dirt.

Among the material that makes up their costumes, a bundle of paper stands out as important – these are the Dolorous Receipts, guarded by these zealots to keep them safe from the Tailor.

The Choir

Spiralling devotees whirl in the dark and the dirt.

Wise TN9. Damage 2/2. Health 3/5. Dealing with them gives the Hunters the Dolorous Receipts.

Dolorous Receipts

Reams of paper stuffed into a leather binder, each a statement of the Tailor’s wickedness – used to enforce a life-long contract. Each time you look at it, it seems as though even more papers have grown from within.

One use. As a Use action: in Close, reduce the Resolve of the Tailor by half its current value, rounding down.

If the Tailor has already been defeated when the Receipts are acquired, then one Hunter may consume them to start a Battle with 1 Focus.

4. The Vestry

Root: The Tailor had a complicated upbringing and some controversial appetites that would see her cast out of polite society; the Bishop kept receipts of her indiscretions, and used them to blackmail her into his service.

Silks, bolts of linen and sheets of fine lace hang from the ceiling in this chamber, but they do little to absorb the noise of the chattering, grinding textile machinery that rattles away of its own accord. Great piles of dye reach as high as the rafters – saffron yellow, rich purple and boreal green – and man-sized spindles of crimson thread blur with the speed of their ceaseless rotation.

What's Next?

Following the Baptism with the Bishop’s ichor, the Hollow begins to fluctuate and collapse without the wickedness that once fuelled it.

Ask the Hunters how they leave the place – do they take a shortcut through the Sanctum? Does a writhing portal burst from the Bishop’s enormous corpse as golden sinkholes threaten to claim their lives? Is it an arduous climb back up through the Root Hole, and out to the surface, and from there an improvised ritual of their own to escape?

Whatever they choose, they leave and emerge in the Refuge – their own version of the Sanctum, an interdimensional coaching inn run by a grumbling landlord bound to the place known as the Keeper. A fire roars in the hearth and the Keeper squints at them as he pours a pint of beer.

“Been wondering when you lot would show up. Sit down. And close the door, will you? You’ll let all the bloody evil in.”

Health: Resolve and Wounds

Resolve is a measure of stamina, determination and physical fitness. Narrate Resolve damage as the target dodging, blocking, shrugging off the pain, becoming tired, losing heart.

Wounds are a measure of how much punishment the target can take before its body gives up. Narrate Wound damage as (gruesome) physical injuries.

A Hunter or Entity with 0 Resolve is Broken. Often, Entities have an ability that triggers When First Broken. If the Entity recovers Resolve and becomes Broken again, this ability doesn’t trigger a second time. Successful attacks against a Broken target inflict the attack’s listed Wound damage instead of Resolve.

An Entity with 0 Wounds is dead. A Hunter with 0 Wounds is dying. If they have any Resolve remaining, they lose it when they are reduced to 0 Wounds. They must succeed on a Hard roll on their turn to revive themselves with 1 Resolve and 1 Wound; if they fail, they die and awaken back at the Sanctum. A Hunter can revive a dying Hunter to 1 Resolve and 1 Wound by making a Guard manoeuvre in their area and forgoing the usual Resolve recovery.
